Few inventions in human history have reshaped civilization as profoundly as the printing press. The ability to reproduce text mechanically—rapidly, cheaply, and in quantity—transformed religion, politics, science, education, and commerce across the globe. # The Press That Remade the World: A History of Printing

Few inventions in human history have exerted as profound and far-reaching an influence as the printing press. Before its advent, knowledge was largely the preserve of a tiny elite—monks, scholars, and aristocrats—who controlled handwritten manuscripts painstakingly copied over months or years. The emergence of mechanized movable-type printing in fifteenth-century Europe set in motion a cascade of transformations that would reshape religion, politics, science, education, and culture across the globe. This essay traces the long history of printing, from its earliest precursors in Asia through the revolutionary innovations of Johannes Gutenberg, and onward through the centuries of expansion, regulation, and eventual industrialization that made printed matter a defining feature of modern civilization.
